evidence_quotes.quote: The status of aquifer knowledge, water access disparities, competing uses, and risks was evaluated from critical literature reviews and data compilation, fieldwork, and analysis of indicator datasets from the Kenya 2009 census.

Data on the sources of water used in the various towns of interest was obtained and compiled from the joint Kenya National Bureau of Standards and the Society for International Development – East Africa county reports that were published in the year 2013, and based on the Kenya Census of 2009, which is therefore used as the base year in this report.

In Kisumu, only the high-income class exceeds the basic water requirement of 60 L/day, while on the lower end are the generally poor informal settlement residents who have a mean per capita daily water use of 22.5 L (Wagah et al. 2010).

Three issues stand out from analysis of national versus county policies, plans and strategies with respect to water, and groundwater in particular: (1) the translation of national policies and strategies into county contexts, (2) lack of expert advice or capacity in water for the formulation of County Integrated Development Plans (CIDPs), and (3) lack of structures and capacity to collect county water data that would be aggregated and assessed at the national level.

A flexible, scalable and transferrable holistic governance and management framework has been developed to guide the formulation of governance and management systems that work effectively and that ensure sustainability.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban domestic water supply sources and water access disparities across five Kenyan towns (Kisumu, Nakuru, Lodwar, Wajir, and Msambweni), alongside groundwater hydrogeology and water quality.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — the report reviews national water legislation and strategies (Water Act 2002, Water Act 2016, NWRMS, NWSS, National Water Master Plan 2030) and five County Integrated Development Plans (CIDPs) regarding groundwater governance and management. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: No — the paper examines macro-level groundwater resource governance, aquifer characterisation gaps, institutional planning coordination, and strategic development plans, and proposes a high-level conceptual planning framework, rather than examining a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing service access).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains descriptive empirical data compilation from hydrogeological fieldwork (geological mapping, geophysical surveys, and consolidated water quality measurements), recalculated 2009 Kenya Census water-source proportions for five towns, and a qualitative critical review of national water strategies and five county development plans, though it does not empirically test a governance-to-access relationship.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive town-level proportions of residents relying on piped water, boreholes, shallow wells, springs, surface water, and water vendors (Table 4), as well as secondary data on per capita daily water consumption and nonrevenue water (Table 5).
criterion_notes.c5: Although urban populations and descriptive water-source distributions are reported from the 2009 census, the paper does not identify or evaluate an empirical relationship between a specific legal/administrative exposure and household or community service access outcomes; the hydrogeological, census, and policy-review components are synthesized only into a conceptual planning framework.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English in Hydrogeology Journal.

study_design: Multi-town case-study synthesis report combining hydrogeological fieldwork and literature review, descriptive secondary 2009 census tabulation, and narrative policy/plan review
population_and_sample: Urban and peri-urban populations in five Kenyan towns derived from the 2009 Kenya Census (Kisumu, n = 439,009; Nakuru, n = 298,254; Lodwar, n = 54,549; Wajir, n = 51,729; Msambweni, n = 22,633), their regional aquifer systems, and associated national and county water policy/strategy documents
exposure: Macro-level national and county groundwater resource governance and strategic planning documents (Water Act 2002 and 2016, NWRMS, NWSS, National Water Master Plan 2030, and County Integrated Development Plans); no rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access
outcome: Descriptive town-level shares of population using different water sources (piped into dwelling, piped, borehole, protected/unprotected shallow well and spring, surface water, water vendor) from the 2009 census and secondary per capita daily water use and nonrevenue water figures
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While the report describes urban water supply sources from the 2009 Kenya Census across five Kenyan towns alongside aquifer hydrogeology and water quality, its governance component is a macro-level strategic policy and planning review (assessing alignment among the Water Act 2002/2016, National Water Master Plan 2030, NWRMS/NWSS, and County Integrated Development Plans regarding groundwater resource characterisation, sustainable yield estimates, and institutional planning capacity) culminating in a high-level conceptual planning framework. Under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, it does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community water service access, nor does it empirically link any such mechanism to an access outcome.
